newsitem.title: INDIA: India says foreign investors can manage broadcasts.
newsitem.headline: India says foreign investors can manage broadcasts.

text.p: Indian broadcast companies could be managed by foreign investors despite a proposed 49 percent cap on foreign equity under a planned law, India's Information and Broadcasting Minister said on Thursday.
Jaipal Reddy told the Foreign Correspondents' Club in New Delhi that a huge demand for capital might end up giving foreign firms effective management influence.
"Indian ownership, though it may add up to 51 percent, is likely to be widely diffused. Foreign ownership could influence management to 49 percent, if not more," Reddy said.
"Corporate laws will determine the degree of management influence."
India is planning to frame before the end of the year a sweeping law to end state monopoly of the airwaves.

There has been strong opposition to opening up broadcast media to the private sector, especially foreign broadcasters. Private producers currently have to rent time slots on state radio and television, or beam through satellites from abroad. They cannot own broadcast stations to air their programmes or acquire broadcast frequencies. News programmes are subject to restrictions.

Last month, Reddy introduced in parliament a draft Broadcast Bill, and sent it to a multi-party committee of lawmakers who are examining the bill amid intense lobbying by foreign and domestic broadcasters.
The bill is expected to be voted on later this year in parliament after the committee proposes changes.

The current bill, described by Reddy as a working draft, bars foreign investors completely from terrestrial, or local, broadcast companies and caps their equity at 49 percent in satellite broadcast firms.
It also proposes severe restrictions on the number of broadcast licences a company can hold and on newspaper companies taking up broadcast licences.
